intro.html: Some words calm things down; these ten stir things up. They describe starting trouble, urging people on, waking them up and feeding feelings until they grow. Several are verbs of motion at heart: agitate means to shake, stoke means to feed a fire, and a goad and a spur were both pointed tools for driving animals forward.

Stirring up trouble: provoke, incite (urge people on), instigate (start it), foment (keep it brewing), agitate (shake up; upset). Urging on: goad (push, often by teasing), spur (urge to go faster or harder), rouse (wake or stir up). Feeding or causing: stoke (add fuel), engender (give rise to).

words.def: to stir up a reaction, especially anger
words.ex: Poking a sleeping cat is a sure way to {provoke} a hiss.
words.ctx: The referee’s strange call {provoked} a storm of boos from the stands; fans who had been quiet all game were suddenly on their feet, shouting.
words.etym: From Latin provocare, “to call forth, to challenge”: pro (forth) + vocare (to call).

mn.cue: pro-VOKE: POKE it and get a reaction
mn.text: Kai tickles the sleeping dragon’s nose with a feather, poke, poke, and he {provokes} a giant, smoky sneeze!

scene.alt: A sneaky boy tickles a sleeping dragon's nose with a feather, and the dragon wakes with a smoky sneeze.

words.def: to urge people on, especially to trouble or violence
words.ex: The prankster tried to {incite} a food fight in the cafeteria.
words.ctx: Instead of calming the angry fans, the loudmouth in the front row tried to {incite} them, shouting that they should rush onto the field.
words.etym: From Latin incitare, “to set in rapid motion, to urge on”: in (on) + citare (to set moving).
words.note: Incite (urge on) is not insight (understanding), though they sound alike.

mn.cue: IN-CITE: urges everyone IN SIGHT on
mn.text: Rex jumps onto a lunch table and yells “Food fight!”, urging everyone in sight to start throwing. He {incites} trouble.

scene.alt: A troublemaker stands on a lunch table shouting for a food fight while two children look shocked.

words.def: to start something, especially trouble; to bring it about
words.ex: Dev {instigated} the snowball fight by tossing the first one at his sister.
words.ctx: Nobody knew who had {instigated} the prank, but someone had started it: every chair in the classroom had been turned to face the back wall.
words.etym: From Latin instigare, “to urge on, to goad.”

mn.cue: IN-STIG-ATE: in an INSTANT, it STARTS
mn.text: Dev throws the very first snowball, and in an instant everyone is throwing. He {instigates} the snowball fight.

scene.alt: A teen throws the first snowball of a snowball fight at a girl, who ducks.

words.def: to stir up trouble or unrest
words.ex: Rumors on the school bus {fomented} a feud between the two grades.
words.ctx: The sly first mate spent weeks {fomenting} unrest among the crew, grumbling about the food and the pay until the sailors were ready to mutiny.
words.etym: From Latin fomentum, “a warm compress,” from fovere, “to warm.” To foment was first to warm a sore; later, to heat up trouble.
words.note: Foment (stir up trouble) is not ferment (to bubble the way yeast does), though both suggest something bubbling up.

mn.cue: FOAM-ENT: stir till trouble FOAMS over
mn.text: Victor stirs his pot of gossip faster and faster, adding a pinch of rumor here and a dash of grumbling there, until it foams over. He {foments} trouble.

scene.alt: A sneaky man stirs a bubbling pot as the word Trouble foams up out of it.

words.def: to push or provoke someone into doing something
words.ex: His teammates {goaded} Kai into singing at the talent show.
words.ctx: Dev didn’t want to race, but his cousins {goaded} him with teasing until he finally lined up at the start, just to prove them wrong.
words.etym: From Old English gad, a pointed stick for driving cattle forward.

mn.cue: GOAD: “GO! GO! GO!” until you do it
mn.text: Rosa’s friends chant “Go! Go! Go!” until she finally steps up to the microphone to sing. They {goad} her into it.

scene.alt: Friends chant and cheer to push a nervous teen toward the microphone on stage.

words.def: to urge on; to push someone to act faster or harder
words.ex: The cheering crowd {spurred} the tired runners toward the finish line.
words.ctx: The news that the library might close {spurred} the neighbors to action; within a week they had raised enough money to keep its doors open.
words.etym: From Old English spura, the pointed tool on a rider’s heel used to urge a horse on.

mn.cue: SPUR: cheers that PUSH you FASTER
mn.text: Jamal is tired in the last lap, but the crowd’s cheers push him to run faster and faster. The cheers {spur} him on.

scene.alt: A tired runner speeds up as children cheer him on from the side of the track.

words.def: to wake someone up; to stir up feelings or action
words.ex: The smell of pancakes {roused} Sami from a deep sleep.
words.ctx: The coach’s speech {roused} the team; players who had been slumped on the bench at halftime leaped up, cheering and ready to play.

mn.cue: ROUSE the HOUSE: the rooster wakes everyone
mn.text: Cock-a-doodle-doo! The rooster crows right outside the window, and the whole house wakes up. He {rouses} everyone.

scene.alt: A rooster crows at the bedroom window, waking a sleepy boy, who stretches.

words.def: to add fuel to a fire; to stir up strong feelings
words.ex: Grandpa {stoked} the campfire until the flames leaped high.
words.ctx: Every new rumor only {stoked} the town’s curiosity about the mysterious visitor, until people were lining up just to catch a glimpse of him.
words.etym: From Dutch stoken, “to feed a fire.”

mn.cue: STOKE it and the flames SOAR
mn.text: Marcus adds another log to the campfire, and the flames leap high. He {stokes} the fire.

scene.alt: A man adds a log to a campfire, and the flames leap higher.

words.def: to stir up or shake; to make someone anxious or upset
words.ex: The washing machine {agitates} the clothes to shake the dirt loose.
words.ctx: The long wait for news {agitated} the families in the hallway; they paced, checked their phones and asked for updates every few minutes.
words.etym: From Latin agitare, “to drive about, to shake,” from agere, “to drive, to do.”
words.note: Agitate can also mean to campaign hard for a change: to agitate for a new park.

mn.text: Theo shakes the snow globe hard, and the snow swirls wildly inside. He {agitates} it.

scene.alt: A toddler shakes a snow globe hard, sending the snow swirling.

words.def: to cause something to exist; to give rise to
words.ex: Her fair rules {engendered} trust among the players.
words.ctx: The teacher’s patience {engendered} confidence in her shy students; by spring, kids who once whispered were reading aloud to the whole class.
words.etym: From Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerare, “to bring to life, to produce”: in (in) + generare (to beget).

mn.text: Nell hands a neighbor a flower; he passes one to Ivy; she passes one to her grandpa. One kind act {engenders} many more.

scene.alt: Three neighbors pass flowers along, one kindness leading to the next.

after.cap: Ten ways to stir things up.

after.html: Two sound-alike traps. Foment (stir up trouble) is not ferment (to bubble, as yeast does), though both suggest something bubbling up. And incite (urge on) is not insight (deep understanding). Notice, too, that engender and spur often describe good things: kindness engenders trust, and good news spurs people to act.

opts.s: The cheering crowd {spurred} the tired runners on toward the finish line.
opts.why: Cheers that urge runners to go faster spur them on.

items.q: The troublemaker tried to ______ the crowd to rush the stage. Which word fits?
items.why: To incite is to urge people on to trouble. Insight, a noun, means understanding.

items.q: True or false: foment and ferment mean the same thing.
items.why: False. To foment is to stir up trouble; to ferment is to bubble and change, the way yeast makes bread rise.

items.q: A coach’s steady praise can ______ confidence in young players. Which word fits?
items.why: To engender is to cause or give rise to. Here it is something good: confidence.

choices: a pointed tool on a rider’s heel
items.why: A spur on a rider’s heel urges a horse forward, so to spur someone is to urge them on.

items.q: Type the verb, from Latin for “to call forth,” that means to stir up a reaction, especially anger.
items.why: Pro (forth) + vocare (to call): to provoke is to call forth a reaction.
